title: Conditional logic toolkit
summary: Translate if, only if, unless and all/no into arrows, chain them, take the contrapositive, and spot the two classic errors.

slides.title: One arrow, read one way
body: A conditional statement says that one thing guarantees another. Write it as an arrow: the sufficient condition on the left, the necessary condition on the right. “If you are in Paris, you are in France” becomes Paris → France.
The arrow only runs one way. Being in France does not put you in Paris. Not being in Paris tells you nothing about France.
The one valid flip is the contrapositive: reverse the arrow and negate both sides. Not France → not Paris. It always says the same thing as the original.
slides.callout: A → B means: A is enough for B, and B is required for A.

slides.title: Translation table
head: The text says
Write
Note
rows: If A, then B / Whenever A, B
All A are B / Every A is B
Only A are B / Only if A, B
A requires B / B is necessary for A
The requirement goes on the right.
A guarantees B / A is sufficient for B
Cross out “unless”, negate what follows it, make it the left side.
Not A unless B / No A without B
“You can’t enter unless you have a ticket”: enter → ticket.

slides.title: Two errors to catch, two quantifier rules

traps.name: Reversal
traps.tell: Treats A → B as if it meant B → A. The answer or argument assumes the necessary condition is enough.
traps.example: Every winner trained daily. Mara trained daily, so she will win.

traps.name: Negation
traps.tell: Treats A → B as if it meant not A → not B. Missing the sufficient condition is taken to rule out the result.
traps.example: Anyone with a ticket can enter. Jon has no ticket, so he cannot enter.

traps.name: Some is not all
traps.tell: “Some A are B” cannot be chained like an arrow, and it does not flip into “some A are not B”.
traps.example: Some lawyers are runners; all runners are early risers. You can conclude some lawyers are early risers, but not that most are.

traps.name: Most plus most
traps.tell: Two “most” statements about the same group do not chain, but most A are B and most A are C does guarantee some B are C.
traps.example: Most voters favor the park and most voters favor the road, so some voters favor both.

slides.title: Level 1: one arrow and its contrapositive
slides.stimulus: Every visitor to the Oriel Museum who carries a backpack into the building leaves it at the coat check. The coat check is staffed by two attendants and is open from nine until five. Today Marcus toured the museum, and he left nothing at the coat check.
slides.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Marcus toured the museum while the coat check was closed.
choices.B: Marcus carried a bag other than a backpack, which he kept with him on the tour.
choices.C: Marcus did not carry a backpack into the building.
choices.D: Marcus is the only visitor today who left nothing at the coat check.
choices.E: Every visitor who leaves something at the coat check carried a backpack into the building.

steps.label: Translate the rule
steps.note: Backpack → leaves it at the coat check.
steps.highlight: Every visitor to the Oriel Museum who carries a backpack into the building leaves it at the coat check.

steps.label: Take the contrapositive
steps.note: Flip and negate both sides: did not leave it at the coat check → no backpack.

steps.label: Apply the fact
steps.note: Marcus left nothing at the coat check. That triggers the contrapositive.
steps.highlight: he left nothing at the coat check

steps.label: Match
steps.note: He had no backpack. Check that the other choices are guesses, or are the reversal.

why.A: The opening hours are never tied to Marcus's visit. This is out of scope.
why.B: Nothing is said about other bags. This adds a fact the text does not give.
why.C: Correct. Not leaving a backpack at the coat check means he had none with him. This is the contrapositive.
why.D: Other visitors are never mentioned, so “only” is unsupported.
why.E: Reversal. Backpack carriers leave them at the coat check; that does not say everyone who leaves something there had a backpack.

slides.title: Level 2: Chain, then apply the contrapositive
slides.stimulus: Every member of the Harlow choir who sings a solo at the spring concert must attend the Thursday rehearsal. No one who attends the Thursday rehearsal can work the Thursday evening shift at the bakery. Priya works the Thursday evening shift at the bakery.
slides.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Priya is not a member of the Harlow choir.
choices.B: Priya does not sing a solo at the spring concert as a member of the Harlow choir.
choices.C: Anyone who attends the Thursday rehearsal is a member of the Harlow choir who sings a solo at the spring concert.
choices.D: Priya does not attend any rehearsals of the Harlow choir.
choices.E: Some members of the Harlow choir work at the bakery.

steps.label: Translate sentence one
steps.highlight: Every member of the Harlow choir who sings a solo at the spring concert must attend the Thursday rehearsal.

steps.label: Translate sentence two
steps.note: “No one who …” gives Thursday rehearsal → not bakery shift.
steps.highlight: No one who attends the Thursday rehearsal can work the Thursday evening shift at the bakery.

steps.label: Chain them
steps.note: Choir soloist → rehearsal → not bakery shift. Contrapositive: bakery shift → not rehearsal → not choir soloist.

steps.label: Apply the fact
steps.note: Priya works the bakery shift, so she skips the Thursday rehearsal and cannot be a choir soloist. Look for exactly that.
steps.highlight: Priya works the Thursday evening shift at the bakery.

why.A: Too strong. She could be a choir member who does not sing a solo; nothing rules that out.
why.B: Correct. Bakery shift → not rehearsal → not a choir soloist. This is the contrapositive of the chain.
why.C: Reversal: soloists must attend, but attending does not make someone a soloist.
why.D: Too strong. Only the Thursday rehearsal is ruled out.
why.E: Nothing says any choir member works at the bakery. Priya may not be a member.

slides.title: Level 3: a missing link hiding in a contrapositive
slides.stimulus: Park permits: Any event held in Mill Park must have a county permit. The permit office has a firm practice: it issues a permit only to organizers who have submitted a noise plan describing how amplified sound will be limited. The harvest fair, a one-day event planned for the second weekend of June, is scheduled for Mill Park. Its organizers did not submit anything to the permit office by the March deadline. Hence the harvest fair will not be held in Mill Park.
slides.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the argument's conclusion to be properly drawn?

choices.A: Organizers who have submitted a noise plan submitted it by the March deadline.
choices.B: Organizers who submitted something to the permit office by the March deadline submitted a noise plan.
choices.C: A noise plan is the only document the permit office requires before it issues a permit.
choices.D: An organizer who submits a noise plan by the March deadline is always granted a permit.
choices.E: The harvest fair's organizers have never before held an event in Mill Park.

steps.label: Translate the premises
steps.note: Held in Mill Park → permit → noise plan submitted. Chain: held → permit → noise plan.
steps.highlight: it issues a permit only to organizers who have submitted a noise plan

steps.label: Contrapositive of the chain
steps.note: No noise plan → no permit → not held. To reach “not held” we need “no noise plan”.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.note: The evidence is “nothing submitted by the March deadline”. The conclusion needs “no noise plan at all”. Those are not the same.
steps.highlight: did not submit anything to the permit office by the March deadline

steps.label: Predict the bridge
steps.note: We need: any noise plan must have come in by the deadline. Then no submission by the deadline means no noise plan.

steps.label: Name the trap
steps.note: B and D both mention the deadline and the plan, but run the arrow the wrong way. They tell us about those who did submit, and we need to know about those who did not.

why.A: Correct. If every noise plan came in by the deadline, then nothing by the deadline means no noise plan, so no permit, so no event.
why.B: Reversed. It says that submitters met the plan requirement. It says nothing about organizers who submitted nothing.
why.C: This restates how permits depend on noise plans. It does not connect the March deadline to the noise plan.
why.D: Wrong group and wrong direction: it tells us what happens to organizers who did submit.
why.E: Past events are out of scope and do not touch the permit or the noise plan.

slides.title: Level 4: a chain mixed with most and some
slides.stimulus: The organizers of the regional conference have released these facts about the registered attendees. Most of the attendees are accountants. Every accountant attending has completed the ethics module, and no one who has completed the ethics module is eligible for the free workshop lottery. Everyone who works at the host firm is eligible for the free workshop lottery. Finally, some of the attendees work at the host firm. The ethics module is offered online and takes about two hours, and the lottery awards places in a free workshop on the final day.
slides.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.A: Every attendee who is not an accountant works at the host firm.
choices.B: Some attendees who have not completed the ethics module are not eligible for the free workshop lottery.
choices.C: Everyone who has completed the ethics module is an accountant attending the conference.
choices.D: Some attendees who are eligible for the free workshop lottery have not completed the ethics module.
choices.E: Every attendee who is not eligible for the free workshop lottery is an accountant.

steps.label: Translate each statement
steps.note: Accountant → ethics module. Ethics module → not lottery. Host firm → lottery. “Some attendees” work at the host firm. “Most” are accountants.

steps.label: Chain and flip
steps.note: Contrapositive of the second arrow: lottery → no ethics module. So host firm → lottery → no ethics module → not an accountant.

steps.label: Use the “some”
steps.note: Some attendees work at the host firm. Each of them is in the lottery and has not done the module. So some lottery-eligible attendees lack the module.
steps.highlight: some of the attendees work at the host firm

steps.label: Name the trap
steps.note: B is almost the same as D. It says the attendees without the module are “not eligible”. That is the opposite of what the chain gives for the host-firm group.

steps.label: The word that kills B
steps.note: The chain proves “eligible”, never “not eligible”, for anyone without the module. A, C and E are reversals or extensions of “some” and “most” into “every”.

why.A: Too strong. Non-accountants might include people who are neither accountants nor at the host firm. “Every” is not supported.
why.B: The word “not” kills it. The only attendees we can place without the module are in the lottery. Nothing forces any without the module to be outside it.
why.C: Reversal. Accountants all took the module, but others may have taken it too, and some may not be attending.
why.D: Correct. A host-firm attendee is in the lottery, so did not complete the module. “Some” is all we need.
why.E: Reversal. Accountants are not eligible, but the argument does not say that everyone not eligible is an accountant.

slides.title: Cheat card
lines: Sufficient on the left, necessary on the right.
“Only if” → right side. “Only” alone → left side.
“Unless”: negate what follows it and make it the trigger.
Contrapositive: flip and negate both sides. Always valid.
Reversal and negation are never valid.
Chain arrows end to end; check a fact against the contrapositive.
